title: Police shoot man armed with knife
article: Two officers were called at 8:30 p.m. to a domestic dispute in a suite at the Machray Apartments, 242 Machray Ave.
After gaining entry to the suite, police were challenged by a man armed with a knife, said police spokesman Const. Bob Johnson.
Johnson said the officers attempted to persuade the man to drop the knife. However, when he became confrontational, police shot him.
A tenant in the building, Bobbi-Jo Oulette, 31, said she knew the couple in the suite and referred to them as Amber and Dan.
"He had just started drinking again after being sober a year," said Oulette.
She said both Amber and Dan had been drinking since Friday, describing it as a binge.
Oulette said that, earlier in the week, Amber sold her some of her furniture to allow the couple to buy more alcohol.
One resident who lives just down the hall from the couple said they were constantly arguing.
"Every second or third day they were fighting," said the man, who refused to give his name.
The man said he heard people running up the stairs of the block, looked out his door, and saw about a dozen police officers.
"Cops were just running everywhere," said the resident.
Moments later, he said he saw a distraught woman standing by the stairwell yelling at cop, "That's my old man."
Another resident who lives below the suite where the shooting occurred said he heard lots of yelling and then several shots.
"I heard the guy yell, 'How could you f---king do this to me,' and then I heard bang bang, bang," said the resident.
Oulette described Dan as an aboriginal man in his mid-20s, and said Amber had been in a car accident as a child and was on disability allowance.
Oulette described the woman as sweet, kind and friendly.
However, she said Amber had been a victim of violence before.
"This is not the first time someone had pulled a knife on her," said Oulette.
Oulette said Amber moved into the apartment block in October. She said the couple had been in a common-law relationship for a few months.

Minutes after the shooting, police swarmed the three-storey building at the corner of Machray Avenue and Charles Street. About half a block was cordoned off and some residents were evacuated from the apartment while investigators pored over the scene.
A transit bus was brought in to keep residents warm.
There have been several shootings involving police officers in the last few years.

Last November, Donald Miles was shot twice in the lower torso by two city police officers after he lunged at them with a knife during a tense stand-off in the parking lot of the Circle K Shell gas bar.
One of the bullets severed a major artery and Donald Miles later bled to death despite efforts of paramedics and Health Sciences Centre emergency room staff to save his life.
In 1997 Abe Hiebert, a local drug dealer, was shot to death when he confronted officers with a baseball bat and pepper spray.

Police are trained to draw and then discharge their sidearms or shotguns when they believe they have no other choice, to control a situation where there's an immediate threat to life, be it to themselves or someone else, or a threat of grievous bodily harm.

Under new police policy, adopted after the fatal shooting of Hiebert, officers involved in shootings are separated by detectives and essentially treated as suspects. They are advised of their rights under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and they must turn over their weapons for ballistics testing.
Once all of the evidence is collected, the city police firearms review board will decide whether the shooting was justified.
If no criminal charges are laid, an inquest headed up by a provincial court judge will be held.
Under the Fatality Inquiries Act, an inquest must be held whenever someone dies because of an act, or an omission, by a police officer in the line of duty.
